Tech Report: A Portrait Photographer Puts 6 Common AI Retouching Myths to the Test

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photographers have plenty of reasons to distrust automatic retouching.
  • DisclosureThis article is brought to you by Reblum.
  • Joe Fraga is a portrait photographer based in Salvador, Brazil, who specializes in professional headshots and has worked professionally for nine years (@joefraga on Instagram).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photographers have plenty of reasons to distrust automatic retouching. We asked Joe Fraga, a portrait photographer in Salvador, Brazil, to test six of the most common ones on real client work and see which still hold up.

DisclosureThis article is brought to you by Reblum.

Joe Fraga is a portrait photographer based in Salvador, Brazil, who specializes in professional headshots and has worked professionally for nine years (@joefraga on Instagram). Fraga has been a Reblum partner since August 2026. All images in this article are Fraga’s own client work, published with permission.

Recent findings suggest that few tools divide portrait photographers like AI skin retouching. To some, it is the only way to deliver a fully retouched gallery on time, from a company headshot day to a family session or a wedding. To others, it means plastic faces, data sent who knows where, and software that only knows what lighter skin looks like.

Industry observers note that some of those beliefs come from experience: early beauty filters and automated tools did earn them. But software changes faster than reputations do. So we asked Joe Fraga to take six of the most common objections and test each one against Reblum, a desktop retouching software for macOS and Windows.

It has been revealed that the images are Fraga’s, and so are the verdicts. Most of them come from his corporate and headshot work, but the same questions apply to family, fashion, event, and wedding photography.

This is the significant one, and it has history. Plenty of retouching software has smoothed faces until the pores vanished, leaving skin that reads as fake from across the room.

In a recent development, reblum is built on frequency separation, the technique professional retouchers use to avoid exactly that. It splits an image into a layer for color and tone and a layer for fine texture, so blotches can be evened out without touching pores, freckles, and fine hair. In Reblum, the General slider removes blemishes and the Texture slider works on the fine texture itself.

I ran a 24-portrait headshot session through Reblum twice: once on the Natural preset at default settings, and once on Fashion with every slider at maximum. Then I compared both versions at 100 percent.

Sources indicate that on Natural, I got the result I need for corporate headshots. The hotspot on the forehead is muted, the redness around the nose and cheeks is calmer, and the pores and the fine lines around the eyes are still there. The beard and eyebrows keep their detail.

Fashion at maximum goes further than most of my clients need. At 100 percent the grain is still there, so it is not the plastic skin this myth describes, but I keep this look for the occasional job that needs a polished finish. For most sessions, I set the sliders at about half and adjust single photos where needed.

Industry observers note that this criticism is serious and well earned. Retouching tools trained or tuned mostly on lighter skin have flattened deeper skin tones.

The usual failures are easy to spot: hotspots that turn gray or matte instead of matching the skin around them, and a tone tool that pulls every skin toward one lighter average. Reblum’s Shine Removal blends in color from the skin next to the highlight, and Tone Balance shifts hue, not luminance, so it does not lighten the skin.

I ran four client portraits across a range of skin tones through Reblum (below), plus the portrait at the top of this article.

The fourth portrait is the hardest case in the set: deep, warm skin with strong hotspots on the forehead, nose, and cheekbones. With Shine Removal and Tone Balance, the hotspots came down without turning gray, the skin kept its warm brown, and his freckles are still visible.

It has been revealed that fraga’s Verdict: Busted. On the deepest skin in this set, the hotspots came down and the skin tone did not shift.

It has been revealed that this objection has three parts, and all three come from real tools. Many AI services process images on remote servers, so photographers ask where client faces go and whether they train someone’s model. Some charge per image or sell credits, which turns any large job, such as a firm headshot day, an event, or a wedding, into a bill. Others make you export everything, edit in a separate app, and import the files again.

Reblum runs on your own computer. Photos are not uploaded, and after a one-time download of the AI model at first launch, it works with no internet connection. The company indicates client photos are not used to train its algorithms. That also means you can retouch on a plane, in a hotel, or on a studio machine kept off the network.

Sources indicate that batch processing is unlimited, with no credits and no per-photo fees, so one portrait and a full gallery cost the same. Reblum works as a standalone app or as a plugin where you already edit: Lightroom Classic, Capture One, Photoshop.

Industry observers note that my workflow is simple. I adjust light and shadows in Lightroom Classic, send the selects to Reblum, and they come back retouched. A typical shoot for me is around 20 photos.

In a recent development, for this test, I took the 24-portrait session from Myth 1 and turned Wi-Fi off. I set the sliders on one image, Reblum applied the same settings to the other 23, and the export took 4 minutes 58 seconds on a MacBook Air M4 at High quality.

Sources indicate that two things to know. Reblum opens DNG files, but it is not a raw processor and does not grade color, so my raw work stays in Lightroom. And batch settings are shared: when one photo needs a different treatment, I switch it to its own settings and adjust it by hand.

Fraga’s Verdict: Busted. The whole session ran offline, with no upload and no credits to count.

It has been revealed that A family portrait or a team photo has faces of different ages and skin types, at different angles and distances. Older tools either missed faces or applied the same heavy treatment to everyone in the frame, from a 6-year-old to their grandmother.

According to recent reports, reblum detects every face in the frame. You can retouch them all at once, or pick a single face and work on it alone, for example clearing a teenager’s skin without touching anyone else.

According to recent reports, I tested it on a team portrait with three people. Reblum found all three faces; you can see them as Face 1 to Face 3 at the top of the panel. The three have different skin tones and different starting points, so I applied one look to the whole frame first and then went face by face. On the woman on the right, for example, I kept Teeth Whitening low, while another face needed more work on the eyes than on the teeth.

According to recent reports, the limit: when you select a single face, Shine Removal and Tone Balance are grayed out, as you can see in the panel. They work on the whole frame only. With three different people in one shot, I would like to set shine for each person. Reblum claims separate Shine Removal and Tone Balance settings for each person are planned for an upcoming patch. That would solve exactly this problem. For now, I set those two in All mode at a level that works for everyone.

Fraga’s Verdict: Mostly busted. It found and handled all three faces, but Shine Removal and Tone Balance can’t be set per person yet.

In a recent development, face-only tools leave a mismatch: a smooth, even face above shoulders, arms, and legs that still show redness and blotches. It happens in any shot with visible skin. Boudoir, swimwear, fashion, and wedding work show it most, but so do personal branding and corporate portraits like the one below.

Sources indicate that reblum evens skin on the face and the body. Its skin segmentation finds the skin and separates it from the backdrop, on close-ups and on wide shots. Refine can be set separately for the face and the body, while Shine Removal and Tone Balance work on all skin in the frame together.

According to recent reports, I retouched a seated portrait that reveals hands and legs. The small marks on the shins and knees are less visible, and the skin on the legs is smoother. The leather skirt keeps its full grain, and the rings and bracelets stay sharp, so only the skin changed.

It has been revealed that the hard highlights on the knee and the shin are softer, but the soft light along the legs stays, so the legs keep their shape. With Tone Balance, the red tones on the knees, knuckles, and toes are weaker, and the hands and legs are closer to one color.

It has been revealed that what it did not do: the veins on the top of the foot are untouched. If a client wants them softer, that is still manual work.

Industry observers note that I would like a separate body control for Shine Removal. The face and the body do not always get the same light: the forehead can have hard glare while the shoulders have only soft highlights. For Tone Balance, one shared control makes sense to me. The tool reads all visible skin together to set the target tone, so face and body match. Separate controls would work against that.

In a recent development, fraga’s Verdict: Busted. Body skin gets real retouching with its own Refine settings. A separate body control for Shine Removal is the one thing I would add.

In a recent development, there are two fears here. One is a single button you can’t control. The other is software that makes the retoucher, and the retoucher’s craft, unnecessary.

On control: each tool described at the top of this article has its own slider. Tools can be used alone or stacked, and any of them can be switched off to compare. The two presets, Natural and Fashion, are starting points, not final looks.

On replacing the retoucher: Reblum claims it handles about 80 percent of the most time-consuming skin work. The remaining 20 percent, a stray hair, a deep crease, very tight close-ups, still needs a person.

In a recent development, before Reblum, I retouched every portrait by hand, in Lightroom and then Photoshop, at 30 to 40 minutes per photo. Today, in the same amount of time, I finish a whole shoot of around 20 photos.

The creative decisions are still mine, too. I handle the initial edits, including exposure, white balance, rough color grading, and the overall look of the images, before moving on to skin retouching in Reblum.

My manual work afterward is mostly on clothing. Sometimes I also remove a distracting detail from the background, or rebuild part of it with a generative tool in Photoshop. Reblum doesn’t at the moment have tools for clothing, and Clean Backdrop is made for studio backdrops, not location backgrounds, so that part of the job is still mine.

According to recent reports, that gap is already starting to close. A clothing retouching tool is coming later this year, with flyaway hair removal planned after that. Both would help reduce some of the manual finishing work that still falls outside the software.

Industry observers note that for now, the biggest change for me is time. The heavy skin work that used to fill most of my editing day is now done by Reblum, leaving me more time to focus on the creative decisions and finishing touches that make each image my own.

Fraga’s Verdict: Partly true. The black box part is busted: every tool is a slider I can see and switch off. The replacement part is half right. Reblum took over the repetitive skin work, not the retoucher. The initial adjustments, color grading, clothing, backgrounds, and final creative decisions are still mine.

Reblum is a retouching tool, not a full editor. Fraga’s tests also turned up a few limits worth knowing before you buy:.

Reblum offers a seven-day free trial of the full app, with no photo limit and no credit card. That is enough time to run your own photos past every myth on this list.

After the trial, it costs $11.95 per month billed yearly, $24.90 billed monthly, or $249 for a lifetime license with all updates. Each license covers two computers, and the yearly and lifetime plans come with a 30-day refund. Download it at reblum.app.

Black Friday offer for PetaPixel readers: from November 17 to November 29, 2026, https://reblum.app/p/PetaPixel gives 50% off a lifetime license and 27% off an annual subscription.

Which myth did we miss? Tell us in the comments.

The TRMNL Frame Is a Gorgeous 31.5-Inch ePaper Picture Frame

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (413 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TRMNL, best known for its ePaper screens, is launching a upcoming product that photographers may find particularly appealing.
  • ePaper picture frames are becoming increasingly common.
  • As TRMNL explains, Frame uses E Ink Spectra 6 technology, powered by TRMNL’s in-house Lazarus color conversion engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TRMNL, best known for its ePaper screens, is launching a upcoming product that photographers may find particularly appealing. TRMNL Frame is the company’s biggest product to date: a 31.5-inch ePaper display built for showcasing art, including photography, in style.

ePaper picture frames are becoming increasingly common. Just last week, Aura released the Ink 10″, its latest digital picture frame featuring an E Ink screen. Last year, InkPoster arrived in sizes from 13.3 to 31.5 inches, the latter of which matches what TRMNL is doing with Frame.

As TRMNL explains, Frame uses E Ink Spectra 6 technology, powered by TRMNL’s in-house Lazarus color conversion engine. E Ink Spectra 6 has six base colors—black, white, red, yellow, blue, and green—and supports up to three additional custom colors. TRMNL says it will release its dithering algorithms as open-source code, too, so people can tinker with Frame for their own applications.

It has been revealed that since it’s designed to beautifully showcase artwork in the home, Frame needs a frame to match. It comes in a handmade wooden body built by TRMNL itself. The organization indicates it opened a woodshop a few miles from its American headquarters for this latest product.

TRMNL says Frame will be available with multiple types of wood, including walnut, white oak, sapele, “and beyond.”.

Frame can be hung in portrait or landscape orientation without any additional hardware and also supports tabletop display via a kickstand.

TRMNL says it’s working with developers on several notable features, including an online art platform where people can submit their work and sell it through TRMNL. Frame is network-connected, of course, although users can also display images via a microSD card. The device recharges via USB-C and, since it’s ePaper, will have an extremely long battery life. It will effectively be a wireless digital picture frame.

As Engadget reports, Frame will begin shipping later this year or in early 2027, and the first batch will comprise around 470 units. Frame will cost $1,300.

Sources indicate that ePaper displays have come a long way in recent years, and while they still cannot match the color reproduction and sharpness of a traditional LCD panel, they do come significantly closer to replicating the look of a paper print. For photographers, there’s a lot to like about the idea of displaying photos on ePaper, especially as dithering algorithms improve.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studio SIGNIFICANT has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.
  • Developed by SUBSTANTIAL in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.
  • The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio SIGNIFICANT has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by SUBSTANTIAL in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be mentioned to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”.

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by BIG to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels said.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

Sources indicate that the first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is right now being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.

Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.

“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.

Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.

“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran said.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

Other spaces designed for refugees include an easy-build playground for children fleeing war, and wooden refugee beds designed to provide more privacy and dignity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

National Geographic has unveiled its Pictures of the Year 2026, a collection of 25 extraordinary photographs revealing the moments, discoveries, and untold stories that defined the past year.

Selected from more than one million images captured by Nat Geo photographers around the globe, this year’s collection offers a striking look at the natural world, human ingenuity, and the remarkable ways people and wildlife navigate a changing planet.

The images transport audiences from the depths of Greenland’s icy waters to the mountains of Peru, capturing moments of wonder, resilience and discovery that might otherwise go unseen.

Made possible by the unmatched access and expertise of National Geographic photographers, the collection embodies the curiosity, discovery, and spirit of exploration that are distinctly National Geographic.

Among the standout photographs are the first-ever images of moray eels spawning in the wild, captured by photographer Tony Wu after nine months in the field in Japan; a climber suspended from a sea cliff in Spain just after a total solar eclipse; and a spine-tingling encounter with a Greenland shark, one of the planet’s longest-lived vertebrates, photographed by Kiliii Yüyan in the 28.4°F waters of Ammassalik Fjord, among the coldest conditions endured by a Nat Geo photographer this year.

For more on this story, visit Nat Geo Photos.

The Best Photos From NASA’s Voyager 1 Spacecraft, Which Is Now 1 Light-Day From Earth

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which introduced on September 5, 1977, is officially one light-day away from Earth.
  • Now about 16 billion miles (around 26 billion kilometers) from Earth, Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach this distance.
  • Sources indicate that to put Voyager 1’s accomplishment into perspective, if someone flashed a light on Earth right now, it would take an entire day to reach the spacecraft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which introduced on September 5, 1977, is officially one light-day away from Earth.

Now about 16 billion miles (around 26 billion kilometers) from Earth, Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach this distance. While space enthusiasts are very familiar with the concept of a light-year, a “light-day” is far less commonly used. However, that doesn’t make it any less impressive.

Sources indicate that to put Voyager 1’s accomplishment into perspective, if someone flashed a light on Earth right now, it would take an entire day to reach the spacecraft. By comparison, light needs just over 130 milliseconds to circle the globe and about 500 seconds to travel from the Sun—which sits nearly 93 million miles (about 150 million kilometers) away.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 is at a truly mind-boggling distance from Earth. As NASA puts it, “Nothing in the universe travels faster than light. Moving through space about 186,000 miles every second, it crosses enormous distances in a given time period, whether it’s a second, a day, or a year.”.

NASA also shared other interesting light-distances. The Moon is 1.3 light-seconds away, even though it took Artemis II astronauts about three days to get there. Neptune, the most distant planet in the Solar System (sorry, Pluto), is about four light-hours and 10 light-minutes away.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 will continue traveling toward AC +79 3888, a star also known as Gliese 445. This obscure star lies more than 17 light-years away, and Voyager 1 is projected to pass within 1.7 light-years of it in a staggering 40,000 years—despite the spacecraft’s cruising speed of nearly 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kilometers per hour).

Recent findings suggest that as for Voyager 1’s sibling spacecraft, Voyager 2, it will reach one light-day from Earth in November 2035. Despite its name and current position behind Voyager 1, Voyager 2 actually rolled out a couple of weeks earlier. However, Voyager 1 took a faster path through the Solar System. Voyager 2 will never catch up.

In a recent development, it’s unclear just how far Voyager 1 will ultimately travel. Theoretically, it will never stop as long as the universe exists. While interstellar dust could slow the spacecraft or potentially even grind it down to nothing, Voyager 1 would have to hit a lot of dust just to cut its speed in half. Something human beings made, touched with their own hands, and launched into space will travel out into the cosmos forever. Humanity will never truly know what happens to Voyager 1, though, as communications are expected to be lost in about 10 years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

Sources indicate that the philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

Sources indicate that for Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

The Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and at the moment serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago.

Recent findings suggest that the current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely upcoming collection,” Grynsztejn claims, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”.

According to recent reports, the MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

According to recent reports, since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she indicates. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”.

An uncontacted tribe in the Amazon rainforest was filmed emerging from isolation to make contact for food in a worrying encounter that highlights the threats to the Indigenous group’s home.

It has been revealed that the Awá are Indigenous people living in the Brazilian Amazon. They are among the last remaining hunter-gatherer communities in the region and one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes. With an estimated population of around 350, many of whom remain uncontacted, the Awá face growing threats from illegal logging and encroachment on their ancestral lands.

According to recent reports, according to a report by nonprofit advocacy group Survival International, 20 members of the Awá people intentionally approached and made contact with local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon on November 17. The Indigenous tribe asked for yams to take back into the rainforest.

Recent findings suggest that footage filmed by members of the neighboring Indigenous Guajajara (Tenetehar) people, who support the government station approached by the Awá, demonstrates a group of men, women, and children standing at the forest’s edge. Partly obscured by vegetation, the tribe appears to be naked and wearing necklaces. The men are seen carrying bows and long arrows.

The Awá are skilled hunter-gatherers who traditionally rely on the forest for food and other resources. However, their territory has faced growing pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and cattle ranchers, raising concerns that increasing encroachment may have forced the group to seek help and food outside the forest.

Unexpected contact with outsiders can pose serious risks to isolated Indigenous groups such as the Awá, who have been described as “Earth’s most threatened tribe.” They are particularly vulnerable to diseases against which they have little or no immunity.

Survival International Director Caroline Pearce said the Awá’s decision to leave isolation highlights how forest destruction and encroachment are threatening the survival of Indigenous communities that have traditionally lived independently.

In a recent development, “This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International’s Director Caroline Pearce indicates in a statement. The uncontacted Awá are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.
  • Dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Zero-Day sci-fi corridor demonstrates an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

Dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

Recent findings suggest that the Zero-Day sci-fi corridor demonstrates an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

Industry observers note that that matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

You can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” noted Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”.

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the firm is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the upcoming cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

According to recent reports, in 2021, Polestar revealed a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

Capture One and Hasselblad have jointly declared that real-time, wired tethered shooting for the X2D II 100C is now supported in Capture One with the latest versions of the camera’s firmware and Capture One software.

Tethered shooting support was announced as in the works back in July when Hasselblad first revealed its partnership with Capture One.

“There is a well-documented history between Hasselblad and Phase One, and we’re not here to dwell on it. Capture One has operated as an independent manufacturer since 2020, and what matters to us is serving photographers,” Capture One’s CEO Rafael Orta told PetaPixel last summer. “And they have asked us for this for years — on forums, in feature requests, in conversations. That’s why we’ve been working for a while with the Hasselblad team to deliver their shooters a native Capture One workflow.”.

Recent findings suggest that now, not only can Hasselblad photographers edit their X2D II RAW files inside of Capture One, the full studio workflow is supported through tethering. Each image will appear on screen at full resolution at nearly the same moment it is captured when connected with a USB tethering cable. Hasselblad states that photographers can check focus and exposure while the set is still live and nobody has moved.

Sources indicate that “[That] means no waiting around or breaking the flow. The full Capture One toolset is available from the first shot, so the grades and masks photographers apply to the first frame carry over to all subsequent shots,” Hasselblad says.

Recent findings suggest that studio photographers don’t need any convincing as to the value of tethering, but those who are less familiar might not know that the capability is hugely vital for commercial sets where clients are on hand. It’s far easier to set clients at a digital tech workstation watching a monitor as results come in rather than hovering over a photographer’s shoulder trying to get a look at the rear LCD.

“This means creative direction and collaboration happen in real time, turning every session into a truly collaborative shoot,” the two companies add.

Sources indicate that “We are always listening to our photographers, and tethering support for Hasselblad cameras was one of the top requests when our collaboration with Capture One was announced earlier this year,” Bronius Rudnickas, Global Marketing Manager at Hasselblad, claims. “We are delighted that this workflow option is now available, giving Hasselblad photographers and creatives worldwide greater flexibility in their creative journeys.”.

Wired tethering for the Hasselblad X2D II 100C is available starting today in Capture One 16.9.1 for desktop and Mobile 4.3.0, requiring X2D II 100C firmware version 1.4.15.7.

Latest Update: Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
  • In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
  • “Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

Industry observers note that but now, Brinkmann indicates his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Industry observers note that greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on new findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”.

In a recent development, the east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann states, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

The rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”.

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail).

Recent findings suggest that vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main.

Sources indicate that the most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

In a recent development, “He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”.

Sources indicate that although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

According to recent reports, “It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann states. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”.

In a recent development, they discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann notes. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”.

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674).

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3.

None of these reliefs revealed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

Sources indicate that the team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann claims. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann claims. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

Recent findings suggest that “The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann indicates. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

It is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann says. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027.

NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app for allegedly using AI-generated images of him in its marketing.

On Tuesday, James filed a lawsuit in the Southern District of New York against the founders of Bron, an AI-powered sports-betting app. The lawsuit focuses on a video ad released by the Bron app’s founders earlier this month. It highlights an AI-generated version of James using the Bron app to bet on basketball games from a locker room.

According to the complaint, the ad depicts James wearing a basketball jersey bearing his nickname and the iconic number 23. It also reproduces his tattoos and a simulated version of his voice. The video indicates the AI-generated figure scrolling through NBA betting options on the app.

“The ad catapulted the Bron app from obscurity to controversy, with the ad gaining a million views within a day — exactly as defendants intended,” James argues in the civil complaint, according to a report by Courthouse News Service.

Recent findings suggest that the complaint also says the AI-generated image of the basketball star “falsely communicates that Mr. James wagers, or considers wagering, on NBA games and NBA player ​performance—conduct that NBA rules prohibit.”.

James argues that the depiction of him sitting in a locker room and betting on basketball could also harm his reputation.

In a recent development, “This is at odds with Mr. James’s well-known and highly televised routine of being on time for games and being one of the first people out on the court,” he argues.

James also claims that the app’s name was chosen to attract attention by exploiting his well-known “Bron” nickname. He accuses PlayVision, the firm that operates the app, and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, of deliberately using the name to mislead consumers into thinking he endorsed or was affiliated with the product.

James’s lawyers sent the company a cease-and-desist letter on November 5. Following the letter, the startup removed the ad from X (the platform formerly known as Twitter) and Instagram and stated it was working to change the app’s name, according to the complaint. However, the lawsuit alleges that the video remained available through third-party reposts and that the company had not changed the app’s name by the time the lawsuit was filed.

LeBron’s lawsuit comes after Norwegian soccer player Erling Haaland sued an airline last month over a social media post that featured an edited image referencing his distinctive hairstyle during the 2026 World Cup.

A photographer had an incredible encounter with a famous grizzly bear known as “The Boss” in Banff, Canada.

In a recent development, jason Leo Bantle was in Banff National Park when he came across fresh bear tracks in the snow. Knowing the substantial bruin must be in the area, Bantle came back on November 6 and spotted The Boss foraging along the railway tracks that run through the park.

“Known for grains being dropped from railcars or other animals being hit, The Boss has learned that when food is not plentiful in the backcountry, the tracks may offer some subsistence,” Bantle tells PetaPixel.

Bantle is aware of the risks of approaching a grizzly in the wild, so he waited at a great distance, observing the bear through an 840mm telephoto lens and binoculars.

It has been revealed that the New York Times ran an article over the weekend about The Boss. It revealed that he is categorized as “habituated” by the park’s management, which means he is not bothered by people so long as he is left alone.

“The biggest thing is his gentleness and his respect towards the people,” Paul Klra, a gas station owner and photographer, told The Times. “He has never done any harm to anyone.”.

Recent findings suggest that while The Boss has never done any harm to humans, he certainly has done harm to other bears. His biggest rival in the area is a bear called Split Lip; The Boss gave him that lip.

He’s also survived being struck by a train and has been known to kill and eat black bears. However, a park ecologist tells The Times that 90% of The Boss’s diet is made up of berries, roots, and other plants.

“As a professional photographer, you are focused on your craft and capturing an image that is the essence of the animal and their environment, so you do lose yourself in the moment,” Bantle says of photographing The Boss.

“I always reflect back on moments like this with The Boss; he is a living legend! The one image of him as he lumbered toward me with light snow falling was just magnificent: the grandeur of this bear, an apex predator, yet the gentleness of his quiet presence — no wind and a light snowfall, it was humbling to be in his presence.”.

The Boss is thought to be 28 years old, advanced for a bear. He has become internationally famous, and it makes the news when he comes out of hibernation.

South London Gallery director Margot Heller to leave role after 25 years

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years.
  • Sources indicate that heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser.
  • “After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for latest adventures in my career,” Heller stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years. Over this time the institution’s physical footprint has more than tripled and visitor numbers increased tenfold, according to a gallery statement.

Sources indicate that heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser. She will retain a connection with the gallery, curating the Dutch artist’s Mark Manders’s first solo exhibition at a London institution, opening at SLG on 23 September 2027.

“After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for latest adventures in my career,” Heller stated in a statement.

“From the day I took up the role, I saw an opportunity to build an institution that could be internationally acclaimed for its contemporary art programme, and deeply embedded in its local community. I have stayed true to that vision ever since.”.

Serge Ramin, the chair of the gallery’s trustees, described Heller as “a visionary curator and cultural leader”, adding: “She leaves a museum that is artistically ambitious, rooted in its community and physically transformed.”.

Heller’s tenure encompassed two major building projects with 6a architects: the conversion of a neighbouring house and construction of an education studio in 2010, followed by the opening of the former Peckham Road Fire Station in 2018.

Sources indicate that the fire station was donated in 2014 by the artist Raqib Shaw, whose identity was initially withheld. Its conversion cost £4m. Heller told The Art Newspaper in 2018 that the gallery had not been actively seeking to expand when the building was offered.

A garden designed by Gabriel Orozco opened in 2016, while Art Block, the gallery’s free space for children and young people on the neighbouring Sceaux Gardens estate, opened at its current site in 2017.

The artist and SLG trustee Alvaro Barrington noted: “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own.”.

He added: “Her commissioning of the Orozco Garden should be considered one of the most important architectural interventions in the UK.”.

Sources indicate that exhibitions Heller has worked on during her tenure include solo presentations by Steve McQueen, Rashid Johnson, Oscar Murillo, Michael Armitage and Christina Quarles. The gallery was a joint winner of Art Fund’s Museum of the Year award in 2020.

According to recent reports, before joining the SLG, Heller worked at Southampton City Art Gallery, becoming its director, and as director of exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery. She was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2014.

The gallery became an independent charity in 2003, having previously been managed by Southwark Council.

Joy Gregory, an artist and SLG trustee, remarked of Heller in a statement: “As a local resident and artist, I am enormously grateful for the extraordinary legacy she leaves behind and excited to see what she does next.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists captured extraordinary footage of two gorillas climbing on each other’s backs and forming a “living ladder” to reach a high branch on a tree that was out of reach.
  • The pair of female western lowland gorillas were filmed displaying what researchers describe as rare behavior in their species: one positioned herself to provide a stable platform while the other climbed onto her back to reach vegetation they could not access individually.
  • Researchers from Tel Aviv University documented the behavior at the Ramat Gan Safari in Israel, recording three separate instances of spontaneous cooperation between the adult gorillas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists captured extraordinary footage of two gorillas climbing on each other’s backs and forming a “living ladder” to reach a high branch on a tree that was out of reach.

The pair of female western lowland gorillas were filmed displaying what researchers describe as rare behavior in their species: one positioned herself to provide a stable platform while the other climbed onto her back to reach vegetation they could not access individually.

Researchers from Tel Aviv University documented the behavior at the Ramat Gan Safari in Israel, recording three separate instances of spontaneous cooperation between the adult gorillas. According to a study published in the journal Primates, the events took place in 2021, 2024, and 2025 and involved the same two half-sisters, Amelia and Lisha.

In each instance, the gorillas performed the same roles. Lisha provided a stable platform, while Amelia climbed onto her back to reach nearby branches. Neither animal had been trained to perform the behavior.

The most extensively documented event occurred in September 2024, when keepers noticed the two females peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. To find out how they had accessed the food, staff reviewed security camera footage.

In a recent development, the recordings revealed a coordinated series of actions. Amelia first walked over and climbed onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha then joined her, standing firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and stretched upward to grasp and break off a branch approximately 15 feet above the ground.

Sources indicate that the combination of the rock, Lisha’s stable position, and Amelia’s additional height allowed her to reach the branch. An electric barrier around the tree trunk prevented the gorillas from climbing it directly.

Michael Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, notes the footage shows genuine cooperation, with Leisha independently choosing to help Amelia achieve their shared goal rather than simply being used as a tool.

“When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia,” Levitzky says in a statement. “She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

Levitzky indicates that gorillas may be more socially and cognitively intelligent than previously thought, and that further research could reveal more about how they cooperate and what this tells us about the origins of cooperation in humans.

“For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes,” Levitzky explains. “As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”.

  • The feature is called Content Protection, and it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Instagram is rolling out a fresh tool designed to help creators identify and manage unauthorized copies of their videos, as the platform responds to growing concerns about content theft and the use of AI to reproduce original work.

The feature is called Content Protection, and it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected. Meta previously introduced a similar tool on Facebook and is now bringing the feature to Instagram.

According to recent reports, once enrolled, creators will receive alerts when Instagram identifies a visual match of one of their original videos. They can then choose to monitor the copied video’s performance, hide it from Instagram and Facebook, add an attribution link directing viewers to the original video, or release their claim and allow the content to remain on the platform.

Recent findings suggest that techCrunch reports that creators who enroll will have upcoming original videos automatically protected. They can also manually select eligible videos published before enrolling. Accounts that have permission to use a creator’s work, such as a second profile or a brand account, can be added to an allow list to prevent their content from being flagged.

Instagram is also expanding its detection capabilities to address AI-generated content. The platform will begin testing a feature that identifies videos using audio from a creator’s original work, including spoken words, even when the original visuals have been replaced with AI-generated imagery.

The manufacturer indicates it is also exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repurpose other creators’ work.

Recent findings suggest that the rollout comes as creators face increasing difficulties protecting their material from AI-generated copies. Videos featuring altered faces, fictional performers, and recreated comedy routines have become a growing concern, particularly for creators whose work is reused without attribution.

Comedian Sarah Purdum tells Mashable she discovered her material had been repurposed by an AI account.

It has been revealed that “It seems to be that female comedians’ work is being stolen and repurposed for sexy AI models,” she notes. “I feel annoyed that my work is being taken for the purpose of drawing in men.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, way back in 2018, Zhongyi (ZY) Optics rolled out the Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 manual-focus lens for the Fujifilm GFX mirrorless camera system.
  • The Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is lighter than its predecessor, has a newly introduced aperture diaphragm, and features an upgraded metal design.
  • The optical design is unchanged, with the lens still sporting 11 elements arranged across seven groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, way back in 2018, Zhongyi (ZY) Optics rolled out the Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 manual-focus lens for the Fujifilm GFX mirrorless camera system. Now there’s an upgraded Mark II version, which is still ultra-fast, manual-focus, and very affordable. It’s also available for Hasselblad cameras.

The Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is lighter than its predecessor, has a newly introduced aperture diaphragm, and features an upgraded metal design.

The optical design is unchanged, with the lens still sporting 11 elements arranged across seven groups. ZY Optics says the lens, which has two High Refractive Index (HRI) and two Ultra-Low Dispersion (UD) elements, delivers “exceptional image quality” with minimized chromatic aberrations.

However, behind the glass is a new 11-bladed aperture diaphragm, up from a nine-bladed unit in the original Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4. ZY Optics claims the new circular diaphragm delivers “rounder bokeh highlights.”.

Sources indicate that with its f/1.4 aperture, the lens is still among the very fastest available for the Fujifilm GFX system. Fujifilm itself doesn’t make any lenses quite as fast—its fastest options are the GF 55mm f/1.7 R WR and the GF 80mm f/1.7, both of which cost over $2,000.

Over on the Hasselblad X system, it’s a similar story. Hasselblad’s fastest lens is the XCD 1,9/80, or, put in more common terms, an 80mm f/1.9 lens. The manufacturer’s 65mm prime is the XCD 2,8/65.

Granted, Fujifilm’s and Hasselblad’s lenses are also native and equipped with autofocus, so there’s that. ZY Optics targets a different market, one less concerned with autofocus and looking to save some money.

In a recent development, the manual-focus prime can focus as close as 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), resulting in a maximum magnification of about 0.25x. Its 65mm focal length delivers a full-frame equivalent of just over 51mm.

Compared to its predecessor, the Mark II lens is significantly lighter. Weighing 900 grams (31.7 ounces), it sheds about 150 grams (5.3 ounces) compared to the original. The lens measures 95 millimeters (3.74 inches) long, accepts a 67mm filter thread, and features a built-in retractable lens hood.

ZY Optics states the latest lens has an improved, precision-machined metal barrel. It looks a little different overall but retains the same general design, with a wide, ridged focus ring and an aperture control ring near the front of the lens. The depth-of-field scale markings have changed slightly, too.

The ZY Optics Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is available now for Fujifilm GFX and Hasselblad X mounts for $599.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Industry observers note that “By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” says a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

According to recent reports, the calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

It has been revealed that according to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735).

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

Sources indicate that meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, says in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC.
  • French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.
  • Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC.

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

In a recent development, think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The upcoming market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”.

Zando Central Market has a rectangular strategy measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

In a recent development, it is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the blueprint, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

It has been revealed that interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

It has been revealed that “This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”.

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC.

New bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border
