💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that few modern artists have proven as reliably sought after as Wassily Kandinsky, the Russian modernist rightfully deemed the father of abstract art, and few have rewritten their own auction record as often.
  • At Christie’s Fresh York’s 20th century evening sale, the sale of Betonte Ecken (1922-23) sent Kandinsky record soaring to $85.8 million, good for nearly double his previous auction high.
  • Sources indicate that in Kandinsky’s view, painters were akin to prophets, and logically, the apocalypse would follow: a cataclysmic collapse of tangible reality, spiritual rapture, and figuration giving way to abstraction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that few modern artists have proven as reliably sought after as Wassily Kandinsky, the Russian modernist rightfully deemed the father of abstract art, and few have rewritten their own auction record as often. The ascent charted here is steady rather than meteoric: records have tended to fall by razor-thin margins, sometimes by less than a million dollars, and in one case, at Sotheby’s London in 2017, the mark was broken twice in under an hour. Each new high nudged the ceiling higher, rather than shattering it outright.

That changed on Tuesday. At Christie’s Fresh York’s 20th century evening sale, the sale of Betonte Ecken (1922-23) sent Kandinsky record soaring to $85.8 million, good for nearly double his previous auction high.

Here is how the market got there.

Sources indicate that in Kandinsky’s view, painters were akin to prophets, and logically, the apocalypse would follow: a cataclysmic collapse of tangible reality, spiritual rapture, and figuration giving way to abstraction. Zum Thema Jüngstes Gericht (On the Theme of the Last Judgment), with its deluge of yellow unleashed upon the canvas, captured the religious fascinations that fueled his creative inquiries. The work is “bristling with the exciting energy of avant-garde abstraction,” our reporter wrote in November 2018, when it appeared at Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern art evening sale (the same sale at which Improvisation on Mahogany set the record benchmark). It sold to an anonymous telephone bidder for $22.8 million, against an estimate of $22 million to $35 million.

Kandinsky’s Study for Improvisation 8 (1909), a cardboard and canvas work, was the highlight of Christie’s November 2012 Impressionist and Modern art auction in New York. The auction house expected it to fetch $20–$30 million, matching the $20.9 million record Sotheby’s obtained for Fugue (1914) in 1990. It was a safe bet: the work sold for $22.8 million.

It has been revealed that fully realized Improvisation studies rarely appear at auction; most of the finished pieces landed in museum collections. The final numbered work in the series, Improvisation 8 is a semi-abstraction set in a hilltop fortress. In it, a man wields a sword in Old Kiev, the medieval district of modern-day Ukraine, amid kneeling pilgrims—mystical spirituality-lite, relative to his later works. The piece was exhibited at Tate Modern, Kunstmuseum Basel, and Fondation Beyeler, but before it came to auction, it had mostly been on loan to the Kunstmuseum Winterthur in Switzerland, where it had hung since 1960.

It’s forgivable to forget the auction record set by Tiefes Braun, one masterwork among many to appear in “Visionary: the Paul G. Allen Collection”, the largest single-owner art auction in history. The sale generated more than $1.6 billion over its two-day run at Christie’s in November 2022 (The opening night alone brought in $1.5 billion.) For a refresher: Tiefes Braun went to an unnamed buyer for $23.2 million. That, along with its history, makes it a significant work, at least by Kandinsky standards.

In a recent development, kandinsky joined the faculty of the Bauhaus in 1922, finding it fertile ground for his experiments in expressive abstraction. Out of them grew Tiefes Braun, a psychological portrait of shape, color and space. According to Christie’s, Tiefes Braun was exhibited widely by Kandinsky through the mid-1920s, and formerly in the collection of the Guggenheim, which acquired it from the estate of the art dealer Karl Nierendorf. Allen, the late Microsoft co-founder, purchased it from the museum in 2000.

According to recent reports, it was no shock that Rigide et courbé broke the artist’s record when it appeared at Christie’s New York Impressionist and Modern sale in November 2016. The 1935 work was estimated to fetch between $18 million and $25 million, placing its $23.3 million finish squarely within expectation. The painting was acquired in 1936 by Solomon Guggenheim directly from Kandinsky and was last exhibited by a museum in 1949. It had been held by the same family since acquiring it at Sotheby’s in London in 1964.

It has been revealed that measuring at 45 by 63.5 inches, the painting “ranks alongside the biggest pictures of his last years,” Conor Jordan, the deputy chairman of Impressionist and Modern Art at Christie’s, said in 2016. Christie’s also said the picture marked Kandinsky’s first experiments with sand. “He may have been inspired by Georges Braque, who often used sand, particularly in paintings from the 1920s and 1930s,” Jordan added.

According to recent reports, improvisation auf Mahagoni (Improvisation on Mahogany) was completed while Kandinsky was putting the finishing touches on his treatise, On the Spiritual in Art, and the two make a perfect pairing. The treatise envisioned non-objective art as the soul’s portrait, compelled onto canvas by spiritual imperative. Improvisation auf Mahagoni is theory in practice: a tapestry of jewel tones applied in staccato brushstrokes, caught mid-pulse like a frozen metronome.

Recent findings suggest that it arrived at Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern art evening sale in November 2018 alongside two other Kandinskys, Le Rond Rouge (1939) and Zum Thema Jüngstes Gericht (1913). Selling for $24.2 million against an estimate of $15 million to $20 million, it proved the most coveted of the three, falling a few million dollars short of the night’s top lots, a Magritte and a Schiele. The painting did, at least, spark “a round of appreciative applause in the York Avenue salesroom,” according to our reporter.

Given the significance of Kandinsky’s “Murnau” works within his artistic evolution, their appearance at auction is a notable event. When Murnau – Landschaft mit grünem Haus (1909) came up for auction at Sotheby’s London in June 2017, the auction house praised it as an elusive “masterpiece,” the work having remained in the same Swiss family collection since the 1920s. It arrived with an estimate of £15 million to £25 million and sold for £20.9 million ($26.5 million), surpassing the artist’s previous auction record of £13.5 million ($21 million) set in 2013.

But as noted below, top lot is a tenuous honor when the competition is the artist himself, and the same sale saw another record broken when Kandinsky’s 1913 Painting with White Lines came to the block six lots later. Both Kandinsky paintings helped push Sotheby’s evening total to £149 million ($187.7 million), a 45% jump from the previous year’s comparable sale, giving the London blue-chip art market a much-needed boost of optimism.

The two top lots on this list speak to the value of Kandinsky’s early 20th-century steps toward abstraction. Tensions calmées, painted decades later, presents a world of biomorphic forms that is far more fantastic. As Sotheby’s noted when offering the painting at its London sale in June, 2021, the work’s formal language is full of contradictions, as its title suggests. “The structural logic of the Bauhaus meets Surrealist fancies that, rather than fight, flow along his soundscape,“ the auction house wrote.

According to recent reports, painted in Paris in 1937, Tensions calmées was one of 50 Kandinsky works famously sold off by the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation in London in 1964—the first in the world devoted entirely to a single modern painter, according to Sotheby’s. (The New York art world, meanwhile, was outraged; a foundational patron of the Guggenheim described it as “a tragedy for the United States,” to the New York Times.).

Willard Gidwitz, of the Helene Curtis family, scooped up the piece, and it spent 57 years in the family’s private collection before his heirs consigned it to Sotheby’s. After brisk bidding, it left the block at £21.2 million (roughly $29.3 million), within its presale estimate range of $24.8 million to $34.4 million, but just enough to break a record.

In a recent development, on October 14, 2026, Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben arrived on the block, heralded by Christie’s London auctioneer Adrien Meyer as “the most important early work by the artist to ever come to auction.” The panoramic procession of peasants, pilgrims, and folkloric beings teeters between figuration and abstraction. The characters are recognizably human but not of this world, rendered in an acidic palette that reads like a psychedelic trip.

According to recent reports, according to our reporting, bidding opened in a flurry, with around 20 competing claims in the opening salvo alone. The most determined bidders were Christie’s specialists Amelia Walker, Katharine Arnold, and Maria Los, with Los ultimately securing the painting on a £27 million ($35.7 million) hammer bid, clearing its high estimate of £25 million before fees. With fees, the final price came to £31.56 million ($41.5 million).

Industry observers note that originally acquired by the Dutch collector Emanuel Lewenstein in 1907, the painting disappeared during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands in 1940. It reappeared on long-term loan at Munich’s Lenbachhaus from the Bayerische Landesbank. In 2023, it was restituted to the heirs of Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann, amid a push from the German government to reunite Nazi-looted art with its rightful owners and following decades of legal action.

Sotheby’s June 2017 Impressionist and Modern art sale in London was one to remember thanks entirely to Kandinsky: the artist’s record was broken twice in less than an hour. First, Kandinsky’s Fauvist-era landscape of Murnau from 1909 went to a phone bidder for £21 million ($26 million). Its reign was short-lived. Six lots later, Painting with White Lines came to the block with a guarantee in excess of $35 million (£27 million) from, if rumors are to be believed, mega-collector Ronald Lauder. A rarely available example of Kandinsky’s foray into abstraction, the picture had left Russia for the first time in 1974, when the Cologne collector William Hack acquired it from the State Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow. His heirs brought it to Sotheby’s.

Four bidders battled for the work, which was ultimately won by an Asian phone bidder for £33 million ($41.6 million) “to thunderous applause—especially from Sotheby’s staff,” according to Artnet News.

Kandinsky’s Murnau mit Kirche II (Murnau with Church II) (1910) depicts the Bavarian village of Murnau, nestled in the foothills of the Alps, in vibrant brushstrokes that experts say heralded Kandinsky’s turn toward abstract art. At Sotheby’s London in March 2023, it set the artist’s auction current auction record of $44.7 million.

Ahead of the painting’s sale, Helena Newman, chair of Sotheby’s Europe, remarked that “Kandinsky’s Murnau period came to define abstract art for future generations, and the appearance of such an important painting—one of the last of this period and scale remaining in private hands—is a major moment for the market and for collectors.” Lucian Simmons, Sotheby’s vice chairman and head of restitution, added that the timing of the sale carried particular weight: 2023 marked the 25th anniversary of the conference that established the architecture for the restitution of artworks looted by the Nazis.

According to recent reports, according to Sotheby’s, the painting hung in the dining room of Johanna Margarete Stern-Lippmann and Siegbert Stern, founders of a textile company and collectors whose vast collection included works by Renoir and Munch, among other masters. After the Nazis rose to power, Stern died, Stern-Lippmann died in Auschwitz, and the collection was looted. In the early 2010s, the painting was discovered at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, Netherlands, where it had been since 1951. A long legal battle ensued, before it was restituted to the 13 descendants of the Stern family in 2022.

“Though nothing can undo the wrongs of the past, nor the impact on our family and those who were in hiding—one of whom is still alive—the restitution of this painting that meant so much to our great-grandparents is immensely significant to us, because it is an acknowledgement and partially closes a wound that has remained open over the generations,” the family said.

Betonte Ecken (1922–23) measures just over four feet square and is marked by dynamic, abstract geometric shapes; the four corners are each pointed to with strong shapes and lines, in keeping with its title, which translates as Accentuated Corners.

Recent findings suggest that the painting has changed hands a number of times. Christie’s provenance shows it first coming to auction at the Jacob Hecht Auction House in Berlin in 1926, from the Schwarz collection, then going to that city’s Galerie Nierendorf, which then sold it, probably in 1929, to Hilla Rebay. She was then the principal adviser to museum founder Solomon R. Guggenheim, an early supporter of abstract art in the US. Guggenheim later acquired it from Rebay, and it remained in the museum’s collection until 1964, when the museum sold it at Sotheby’s London to Upcoming York art dealer Stephen Hahn. At some point, Hahn sold it to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar, who put it up for auction at Sotheby’s in 1986, when it went to the Nahmads.

On November 17, the painting changed hands again, when it sold at Christie’s 20th-century evening art sale. It hammered for $74 million; with the house’s fees, the final sale amount was $85.8 million. The work sold after a short bidding war between Christie’s global president Alex Rotter, Sara Friedlander, chairman of post-war & contemporary art, Americas at Christie’s, and art advisor Ralph De Luca. Rotter came away the victor, with the winning $74 million bid. —Brian Boucher.

What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns.
  • Sources indicate that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build.
  • Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Sources indicate that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

Recent findings suggest that from those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:.

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research indicates that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Sources indicate that significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

In a recent development, if you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

It has been revealed that you know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Industry observers note that every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

  • Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.

Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

“Through exploring the material’s qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered,” Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

“Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile,” added Arnaiz.

“Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications.”.

With Bianni, Arudeko aimed to uncover the hidden value of discarded wool whilst reimagining the ancient material’s ancestral history and “cultural memory”.

“Bianni was born from the idea of giving newly introduced life to the leftover wool from our rug and cushion production in Oaxaca,” remarked Arnaiz. “This wool carries within it the knowledge of the artisans who work with it, as well as the colours of the earth embedded in its fibres.”.

Arnaiz explained that the material is made purely from natural materials, with no additives.

Industry observers note that “No additives, just natural materials – why mix these fibres?” she said. “Not only for an aesthetic purpose, as wool brings fire resistance to the paper.”.

Throughout the process, the studio aimed to minimise water consumption and carbon dioxide production as much as possible. Bianni’s production was also kept local to reduce transport needs whilst supporting the local community.

By working with artisans from rural communities and blending traditional craft knowledge with contemporary design practice, Bianni aims to champion historic crafts whilst fostering long-term community development and economic inclusion.

Other wool projects recently featured on Dezeen include waste-wool cladding designed for retrofits and a collection of rugs with architectural designs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Christie’s 20th-century art sale on Tuesday night, a painting by Russian-born pioneer of abstraction Wassily Kandinsky notched a new high at auction when it hammered for $74 million; with the house’s fees, the final sale amount was $85.8 million.

Betonte Ecken (1922–23) carried a $60–$80 million estimate and was guaranteed to sell by the house, financed in full or in part by a third party, as noted in the sale catalogue. Christie’s confirmed to ARTnews ahead of the sale that it was bound to sell at a record-setting level. It was tied for the highest-estimated lot in the house’s marquee November sales with a landscape by Austrian market titan Gustav Klimt, also on Tuesday. Related Articles Rare Artist-Designed Louis Vuitton Handbags Included in Upcoming Christie's Upcoming Online Sale Amid Legal Controversy, Christie's Withdraws Frida Kahlo Painting Hours Before Auction.

According to recent reports, the work sold after a short bidding war between Christie’s global president Alex Rotter, Sara Friedlander, chairman of post-war & contemporary art, Americas at Christie’s, and art advisor Ralph De Luca. Rotter came away the victor, with the winning $74 million bid.

The seller was the prominent Lebanese-American Nahmad family, which acquired the canvas at Sotheby’s Latest York in 1986, ARTnews revealed in October; according to Sotheby’s, it hammered at that sale for $1 million. (It had also come to market at the same house in 1964, when it hammered for $61,000.) The art-dealing dynasty’s holdings are reputed to include as many as 5,000 artworks, collectively worth upwards of $4 billion.

It has been revealed that kandinsky’s previous high was $44.8 million, paid for the artist’s 1910 painting Murnau mit Kirche II (Murnau with Church II) at Sotheby’s London in 2023. Some 14 Kandinsky canvases have fetched prices north of $20 million since 1990, according to the Artnet auction price database; all but one has sold since 2012. His third-highest price, $41.8 million, was achieved in October, when Christie’s London sold his 1907 painting Das Bunte Leben (La vie mélangée).

Betonte Ecken measures just over four feet square and is marked by dynamic, abstract geometric shapes; the four corners are each pointed to with strong shapes and lines, in keeping with its title, which translates as Accentuated Corners.

Sources indicate that the painting has changed hands a number of times. Christie’s provenance shows it first coming to auction at the Jacob Hecht Auction House in Berlin in 1926, from the Schwarz collection, then going to that city’s Galerie Nierendorf, which then sold it, probably in 1929, to Hilla Rebay. She was then the principal adviser to museum founder Solomon R. Guggenheim, an early supporter of abstract art in the US. Guggenheim later acquired it from Rebay, and it remained in the museum’s collection until 1964, when the museum sold it at Sotheby’s London to Fresh York art dealer Stephen Hahn. At some point, Hahn sold it to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar, who put it up for auction at Sotheby’s in 1986, when it went to the Nahmads.

Born in Moscow in 1866, Kandinsky published the book On the Spiritual in Art in 1911 and was part of the influential Blaue Reiter group. After his first solo exhibition, at Der Sturm gallery in Berlin in 1912, one of his works was included in the groundbreaking 1913 Armory Show exhibition in Newly introduced York. He lived in Russia from 1914 to 1921, mainly in Moscow, where he maintained a position at the People’s Commissariat of Education, until moving to Weimar in 1922. His first New York solo was in 1923, organized by Société Anonyme, the organization founded in 1920 by Marcel Duchamp, Katherine Dreier, and Man Ray.

Kandinsky became a German citizen in 1928, but would relocate to France when the Nazi government closed the Bauhaus in 1933, becoming a French citizen in 1939. The Nazis seized dozens of his works in the party’s campaign against “degenerate art.” Kandinsky died in France in December 1944, three days short of his 78th birthday and six months shy of Germany’s surrender to Allied forces.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

The organization said the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

“When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey,” noted Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

“It’s important to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other challenges are not always apparent,” she continued. “Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed.”.

“Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor,” Tophof said.

People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn’s usually need to track their daily bowel symptoms.

A secondary target market is competitive athletes and fitness enthusiasts, who Kohler claims can use the hydration data to make training adjustments.

Dekoda is compatible with most toilets. It has a simple flattened capsule shape in gleaming white polycarbonate and attaches to the outside of the rim with an adjustable clamp.

On the other side of the clamp, a customised camera points down into the bowl, using spectroscopy to detect the colour and consistency of urine and stool.

To withstand the bathroom environment, the exterior of the device is made of a polycarbonate that is antibacterial and chemical-resistant, while the mechanical components are made of stainless steel.

According to recent reports, A specially trained algorithm analyses the collected data and insights are viewed in the accompanying Kohler Health app. It automatically tracks bathroom routines and identifies trends, while users can also add information about their meals, medications and exercise to add context, and share insights directly with their doctor when they desire.

People’ data is encrypted as it travels between their devices and Kohler’s systems but decrypted and processed to provide the service.

Kohler Health stated Dekoda, which was released in October 2025, is helping destigmatise the collection of gut health-related metrics, which individuals could previously only monitor through test strips or stool samples.

It is part of a small wave of fresh devices focused on analysing the body’s fluids, from spit to menstrual blood, as wellness technology expands beyond watch-style heart rate monitors and activity trackers.

#33726. Tech Report: The Most Expensive Works by Gustav Klimt Sold at Auction

Tech Report: The Most Expensive Works by Gustav Klimt Sold at Auction

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction.
  • The market for Klimt reached newly introduced heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces.
  • Klimt’s highest results now count among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 11 paintings discussed below.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. From the gilded elegance of his celebrated portraits to the richly patterned views of Lake Attersee completed during his summer retreats, Klimt’s oeuvre embodies the decorative brilliance and artistic innovation that defined Viennese Modernism. The rarity and enduring appeal of these works among collectors have made them some of the most valuable examples of early 20th-century art ever offered for sale.

The market for Klimt reached newly introduced heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces. On Tuesday, Christie’s added another landmark sale to the list, when it sold the 1915-1916 landscape Litzlbergkeller for $82.3 million.

Klimt’s highest results now count among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 11 paintings discussed below.

Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee) depicts the forester’s house at the entrance to Austria’s Weißenbach Valley, where Gustav Klimt stayed during his summers on the southern shore of Lake Attersee. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity.

In a recent development, created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. Offered at Sotheby’s New York on November 5, 2003, with an estimate of $18–25 million, the painting achieved $29.1 million. The result confirmed the growing appreciation of Klimt’s landscapes, now regarded as some of the artist’s most personal and innovative achievements.

Sources indicate that klimt’s Apple Tree I is a luminous example of his mature landscapes, depicting a single apple tree rising above a dense carpet of flowers and foliage. This oil on canvas is distinguished by its vibrant palette, shimmering brushwork, and richly decorative surface, reflecting Klimt’s interest in nature during his summers at Lake Attersee and the influence of Vincent van Gogh’s expressive approach to color and movement.

It has been revealed that first exhibited at the Große Kunstausstellung in Dresden in 1912, the work demonstrates Klimt’s ability to turn a simple natural motif into a striking decorative composition. Its provenance includes ownership by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and its restitution to their heirs in 2006. Offered at Christie’s Latest York with an estimate of $15–25 million, Apple Tree I sold for $33 million on November 9 of that same year. The sale underscored the enduring appeal of Klimt’s garden landscapes.

Sources indicate that from 1900 until his death in 1918, Klimt often spent his summers in the Austrian countryside on the shores of Lake Attersee,. It was during his summers there, in Litzlberg, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. The 1915-1916 canvas Litzlbergkeller presents a view focused on the Litzlberg Cellar, a brewery and inn on the north shore where Klimt stayed during his first several summers in the area, but actually dates from a decade after his move to a cottage on the lake’s southern shore. The artist partly based the composition on his own study via a telescope from the opposite shore and partly on postcard views.

The piece was commissioned by banker and entrepreneur Otto Primavesi, who, with his wife Eugenia, was a major patron of the arts and commissioned Klimt to paint two family portraits in 1912. It went by 1927 to Austrian photographer and anthropologist Hugo Bernatzik; then to Vienna collector Kurt Wieser, who owned it from the ‘30s until at least 1958; and from there to Serge Sabarasky, a cofounder of Latest York’s Neue Galerie and a major promoter of Klimt’s work. In its long life, it has hung on the walls of museums and institutions such as Secession Vienna; the Künstlerhaus in Vienna; the Musées Royaux des Beaux-Arts in Brussels; Palazzo Strozzi in Venice; Kunsthaus Zürich; and the Leopold Museum in Vienna.

It has been revealed that in May 1997, Sotheby’s Upcoming York sold the work from the estate of Sabarsky, who died in 1996, for $14.7 million. Adjusted for inflation, that’s about $30.9 million On November 17, the work returned to the auction block at Christie’s, where global president Alex Rotter, and Max Carter, the house’s global chairman, battled for the work in an extended five-minute back-and-forth. The work hammered at $71 million, with Rotter taking the winning bid. With the house’s fees, it fetched $82.3 million. —Brian Boucher.

Klimt’s Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II is an oil on canvas depicting the eponymous Viennese socialite and salonnière, who was one of Klimt’s most notable patrons and the only sitter to whom he devoted two paintings. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie Newly introduced York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case.

In a recent development, on November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s Upcoming York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. In 2016 the work was sold privately by its owner, Oprah Winfrey, who had purchased it at Christie’s, to an anonymous Chinese buyer for a reported $150 million, making it one of the most significant private art transactions of the decade.

“I get up early in the morning, usually around 6 am, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. If I get up and the weather is fine, I go into the nearby forest. I am painting a small beech grove, mixed with a few conifers,” wrote Klimt in a letter to M. Zimmerman in August 1903. In Birch Forest (Buchenwald), he captured a secluded grove with precision. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface.

Recent findings suggest that landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. With each tree trunk bearing its own unique markings, the painting reveals extreme attention to detail. Acquired by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and confiscated by Nazi forces, Birch Forest was returned to their heirs in 2006 before appearing at Christie’s Upcoming York on two occasions. In November 2006, the lot achieved $40.3 million against an estimate of $20−30 million. Returning to the auction house as part of the Paul G. Allen Collection in 2022, it realized $104.6 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time.

Recent findings suggest that litzlberg am Attersee depicts the shoreline of Lake Attersee, with houses nestled beneath a densely wooded hillside and a narrow stretch of water in the foreground. Recent scholarship suggests the painting was executed in the second half of 1914. Its vibrant palette, flattened perspective, and densely layered brushwork exemplify Klimt’s decorative approach to landscape. The composition is believed to have drawn in part on a postcard photograph of the lake that the artist sent to his nephew in August 1914.

Acquired directly from Klimt by Viennese patrons Viktor and Paula Zuckerkandl, the painting later entered the collection of Viktor’s sister, Amalie Redlich, a Jewish collector who was dispossessed following the Nazi annexation of Austria and deported to Łódź in 1941. After decades in the collection of the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, the work was restituted to Redlich’s heir in 2011. Later that year, it sold for $40.4 million at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York, surpassing its $25–30 million estimate. A portion of the sale proceeds was donated to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg to support an extension named in Redlich’s honor.

Industry observers note that klimt’s Bauerngarten (Blumengarten) (Flower Garden), one of the artist’s most celebrated landscapes, presents an informal profusion of poppies, daisies, zinnias, and roses arranged into a riot of color and pattern. This oil on canvas gives a sense of Klimt’s summers at Lake Attersee and of his evolving approach to landscape, rooted in the symbolic ambitions of the Viennese avant-garde. Painted in the garden of the Mayr-Hof, his summer retreat in Litzlberg, the work indicates how the natural and decorative worlds converged under his brush.

According to recent reports, first exhibited at the Kunstschau in Vienna in 1908, the painting attracted attention for its innovative composition and almost mystical treatment of nature. Offered at Sotheby’s London in 2017 with an estimate in excess of $45 million, Bauerngarten sold for approximately $59.3 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time. The sale underscored the rarity of major Klimt landscapes appearing on the market, with many works of this caliber held in museum collections.

A young woman clad in a flower-patterned cape sits in a frontal pose against a vivid red background. Her face is rendered with delicate, precise details that contrast with the looser, more expressive brushwork characteristic of Klimt’s late style. The identity of the sitter remains uncertain. Earlier catalogues identified her as Margarethe Constance Lieser (1899−1965), while more recent research has suggested that she may have been either Helene Lieser (1898−1962) or Annie Lieser (1901−1972), daughters of the Viennese patrons Henriette and Justus Lieser. Klimt began working on the portrait in 1917, with the model visiting his studio in Hietzing nine times during April and May of that year. The portrait was unfinished when he died of a stroke on February 6, 1918.

The painting was known to scholars only through a black-and-white photograph, and its whereabouts remained uncertain for decades before it was discovered in Austrian private hands. On April 24, 2024, it was auctioned by Vienna’s im Kinsky, Austria’s second-largest auction house, recognized for its expertise in Klimt’s works and its experience handling restitution-related art sales. Portrait of Fräulein Lieser sold for approximately $41 million including fees, setting a record as the highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction in Austria. The sale was conducted on behalf of the owners at the time and the legal successors of the Liester family, following an agreement based on the 1998 Washington Principles. The work was purchased by Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous buyer.

According to recent reports, dame mit Fächer is thought to be the last portrait Klimt worked on before his death in 1918; it was still on the easel in his Vienna studio at the time of his passing. The work represents the culmination of the artist’s late portraiture, combining the human presence of the unidentified sitter with the rich patterns and decorative experimentation that defined his last years. Returning to the square format he first employed in Portrait of Sonja Knips (1898), Klimt placed the figure at the center of the composition and surrounded her with motifs drawn from Asian art, including the phoenix and lotus blossoms. The sitter’s elaborate robe also evokes Klimt’s long-standing interest in textiles and fashion, an area closely connected to his companion Emilie Flöge, an influential Viennese fashion designer.

Industry observers note that at Sotheby’s London in June 2023, Dame mit Fächer carried an estimate of more than £65 million ($80 million) and was backed by a third-party guarantee. The painting was hammered in at $93.5 million, reaching $108.4 million with fees and establishing a latest auction record for Klimt. The result surpassed the previous record of $104.6 million held by Birch Forest, highlighting the extraordinary demand for Klimt’s late masterpieces in the international market.

In this painting of the meadows surrounding Lake Attersee, Klimt moves away from a traditional landscape format to offer a dazzling carpet of wildflowers—bellflowers buttercups, daisies, cornflowers, clover, and dandelions—that fills the canvas, Here, the horizonless view, square composition, and flattened pictorial space show the influence of late Claude Monet, Japanese art, and emerging Modernist photography.

Executed likely in the summer of 1908, Blumenwiese represents a pivotal moment in Klimt’s landscape painting, when he pushed the genre toward greater abstraction. The radical composition was so unconventional that some contemporary critics dismissed Klimt’s style as the work of a “madman.” Its distinguished provenance, including ownership by Austro-Galician painter Broncia Koller-Pinell and her husband, Hugo Koller, further enhances its historical significance. The painting sold at Sotheby’s in 2025 for $86 million (including fees), becoming the second-most expensive Klimt landscape ever auctioned and reaffirming its rarity and enduring appeal among collectors.

Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914−16) exemplifies Klimt’s mature portrait style, where realism and decoration meet seamlessly. The subject emerges from an elaborate costume that blurs the boundary between figure and background. Completed after nearly three years of revisions, the painting demonstrates Klimt’s meticulous working process and extraordinary feeling for ornamentation.

Commissioned by the Lederer family, among Klimt’s most important patrons, the painting is one of only two full-length portraits by the artist remaining in private hands. It survived Nazi confiscation during the Second World War and was restituted in 1948. Its provenance, later including a time in the collection of Leonard A. Lauder, makes it one of Klimt’s most significant surviving mature portraits. Estimated at $150 million, the painting was the centerpiece of Sotheby’s November 2025 sales. After a dramatic 20-minute contest between two telephone bidders, it realized $236.4 million (including fees), eclipsing Klimt’s previous record and becoming the second-most expensive work ever sold at auction, behind Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the fourth generation iPod – the last model to feature a monochrome screen.
  • In a recent development, after a week with the iPhone Duo, I'm, well, smitten again.
  • I'll be exploring how the iPhone Duo fares for specific creative tasks over the coming weeks, but today I want to talk specifically about the design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I remember my first Apple product. It was the fourth generation iPod – the last model to feature a monochrome screen. For a few years I'd backed the wrong horse, thinking Sony's minidisk players were the future of portable music. But as soon as I held the iPod, I was smitten. It felt like it had fallen out of the future, and like it was designed just as much to be looked at as it was to be used. And for the first time in decades, I'm feeling the same way about a upcoming Apple product.

In a recent development, after a week with the iPhone Duo, I'm, well, smitten again. After years (and years) of incremental upgrades, we finally have something that feels genuinely newly introduced and exciting. And if you can swallow the huge asking price, I think this might be the ultimate smartphone for creatives.

I'll be exploring how the iPhone Duo fares for specific creative tasks over the coming weeks, but today I want to talk specifically about the design. This thing feels truly luxurious. With its gleaming metallic finish and satisfyingly compact proportions when closed, it reminds me somewhat of a vintage cigarette holder. There's something almost Art Deco about it. Foldables have always felt awkward, but Apple has somehow made it elegant.

Sources indicate that speaking of size, I've seen plenty of online commentators complain that the Duo is too small (Apple is even rumoured to be working on a larger version). But for me, it's perfect. As someone who prefers phones that don't require three hands to hold, I've always been one of the few defenders of the iPhone mini. For me, its diminutive dimensions are precisely the point. After years of phones getting progressively more enormous, there's something wonderfully refreshing about a device that actually wants to fit in your pocket.

Sources indicate that but of course, the real headline here is the larger internal display. This has been the subject of debate too, thanks to the matte nano-texture layer. This does take some getting used to (and in my experience, seems a little harder to clean), but there are massive benefits too – namely, vastly reduced glare. And perhaps even more importantly, it makes the dreaded 'crease' less visible.

There are some delightful software touches that make the Duo a joy to use. The open/close animation, which blurs content as the screen is folded or unfolded, is subtle way of explaining that content is moving from one screen to another. And my personal favourite touch is the newly introduced StandBy mode, which works when the phone is propped in 'tent' mode, turning it into a desk calendar and clock.

Recent findings suggest that as a creative, the possibilities of the Duo are immediately appealing. Having more room to view images, browse design inspiration or work with visual content without reaching for a separate tablet feels like a meaningful improvement, rather than another feature invented to fill a keynote. I'll be exploring the creative potential in more detail soon. But for now, after just a few days with the device, it's clear that Apple's sense of fun is well and truly back. This is a bold yet playful product design that feels, for the first time in forever, like it has fallen out of the future.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he indicates.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he indicates.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe claims. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”.

Industry observers note that nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he claims.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe claims.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that jeff Koons has long been an art collector.
  • Recent findings suggest that collectors and the public are getting another look at that collection this week.
  • Sources indicate that seven of the works, grouped under the title “Heroes and Lovers,” were offered at the house’s 20th-century art sale on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jeff Koons has long been an art collector. As far back as 2010, when the Latest York Times visited “one of the world’s most famous living artists,” his Upper East Side home held works by artists ranging from the French Realist Gustave Courbet and the Rococo painter Jean-Honoré Fragonard to the Impressionist Édouard Manet and the 16th-century Antwerp painter Quentin Massys. He had generally avoided discussing his collection, the Times wrote, “out of discretion and privacy.”.

Recent findings suggest that collectors and the public are getting another look at that collection this week. Nine works consigned to Christie’s Fresh York came from the artist’s holdings, according to two unnamed industry sources who spoke to the Times this fall. The sources stated the house had guaranteed Koons a minimum price and that he planned to plow the proceeds toward his famously expensive art production. (Christie’s has identified the seller only as “a distinguished collector.”) Related Articles A Wassily Kandinsky Sold by the Nahmads Fetches $85.8 M. at Christie's, Notching a New Auction High Rare Artist-Designed Louis Vuitton Handbags Included in Upcoming Christie's Upcoming Online Sale.

Sources indicate that seven of the works, grouped under the title “Heroes and Lovers,” were offered at the house’s 20th-century art sale on Tuesday. Together they were estimated at $104 million to $153.5 million. The low end alone is slightly more than the $91.1 million Christie’s got in 2019 for Koons’s own 1986 sculpture Rabbit. The other two works will be offered during the house’s Classic Week next year.

Sources indicate that the group did not perform particularly well in the end, hammering for a total of just $87.8 million in total, well shy of the low estimate; with the house’s fees, the group sold for $104 million. No lot exceeded its estimate; four fell short of their low estimates. Four of the works sold at an inflation-adjusted loss.

Recent findings suggest that leading the pack with four works, including the top-estimated piece, was Pablo Picasso; the sale also included examples by Fragonard, Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem, François Le Moyne, Édouard Manet, and Tilman Riemenschneider.

In a recent development, accounting for up to 60 percent of the total estimate for the sale was Picasso’s Le Baiser (1969), showing two lovers entwined in a kiss and estimated at $40 million–$60 million. Koons bought it at Sotheby’s in 2008 for $17.4 million ($27.1 million, adjusted for inflation). It has hung on the walls of institutions from the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris to London’s National Gallery and Latest York’s Guggenheim Museum. But the splashy provenance and exhibition history couldn’t get it to its low estimate. It hammered for just $26.5 million to a man bidding in the room, to sell for $31.2 million with the house’s fees.

Sources indicate that picasso’s 1941 canvas Tête de femme (Dora Maar), showing the photographer who was then his lover, was estimated at $25 million–$35 million. Koons acquired it in 2007 at Christie’s New York for $16.3 million ($26.1 million, adjusted for inflation). It barely squeaked by its low estimate to hammer at $25.5 million to the house’s Katharine Arnold, vice-chairman and head of post-war and contemporary art, selling for $30 million million with fees.

He purchased the Spaniard’s Couple (1969), showing a duo in an embrace, at Sotheby’s London in 2011, paying $10.5 million ($15.8 million, adjusted for inflation); it was estimated at $12 million–$18 million. It had not been exhibited since a 1970 show at the Palais des Papes in Avignon, France. It hammered for $13 million to Christie’s global president Alex Rotter, or $15.6 million with fees.

In a recent development, the Spanish artist’s Tête de femme (1939–40) was estimated at $10 million–$15 million. The piece had passed through the hands of the legendary American collectors Burton and Emily Tremaine in the 1940s and the dealer Larry Gagosian in the ’80s. Koons acquired it at Sotheby’s Paris in 2012 for $7.9 million ($11.5 million, adjusted for inflation). It hammered to deputy chairman Olivier Camu for just $6 million, to sell for $7.4 million with fees.

In a recent development, bound to set a record was the Dutch painter Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem’s 8-foot-wide canvas Hercules and Achelous (1590), which was estimated at $12 million–$18 million. The artist’s previous high was $8.1 million, achieved by the same painting at the same auction house in 2008, when Tuesday’s seller acquired it. It was on loan to Upcoming York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art from then until 2018. That $8.1 million far exceeds the artist’s second-highest price, $1.7 million, set with The Raising of Lazarus (1602) at Christie’s London in 2023. It hammered to Andrew Fletcher, global head of the old masters department, for $11.5 million, just shy of its low estimate, to sell for $13.9 million with fees.

Industry observers note that A wooden sculpture by the German artist Tilman Riemenschneider, Saint Catherine (ca. 1505), bore a $4 million–$6 million estimate. Koons bought it at Sotheby’s New York in 2008 for $6.3 million ($10 million, adjusted for inflation), setting the artist’s still-standing record, and then lent it to the Met, where it remained on view until 2019. (That price is double his second-highest, which is, in turn, nearly six times his third-highest.) It hammered within estimate for $4.5 million to François de Poortere, head of old masters for New York, or $5.6 million with fees, shy of what Tuesday night’s seller paid for it.

It has been revealed that the cheapest piece on offer from the Koons trove was a Manet pastel, Femme au tub (ca. 1878–79), estimated at $1 million–$1.5 million. Koons paid $2.3 million for it at Sotheby’s London in 2014 ($3.3 million, adjusted for inflation). He lent it to a show that appeared at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Getty and to another at the Met. It hammered shy of the low estimate at $800,000, or $1 million with fees, less than half what the seller paid for it.

In a recent development, the S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

Industry observers note that the index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a manufacturer is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

It has been revealed that an S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. organization. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

Sources indicate that the data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Sources indicate that warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals.".

Recent findings suggest that the top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

It has been revealed that the lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

Recent findings suggest that blackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, debuted in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:.

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

Recent findings suggest that the most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard highlights that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly states to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right.".

Industry observers note that transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

It has been revealed that if you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

It has been revealed that VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

Recent findings suggest that either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

Sources indicate that as little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

It has been revealed that S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

Sources indicate that S&P 500 index funds are the single most important building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

Industry observers note that you might be suffering whiplash if you've been watching things at Etsy lately. Just a couple of weeks ago, things looked tentatively hopeful for the marketplace as Etsy promised to crackdown on AI slop. Now creators are fleeing the platform in droves because of its own AI policy.

A post shared by Aaron Millard (@aaronmillardillustration).

A post shared by Cognitive Surplus (@cognitivesurplus).

A post shared by aaron meshon (@aaronmeshon).

A post shared by Elena Skoreyko (@elenaskoreyko).

A post shared by Elisa | Kunst & Design fresh from the forest (@hohwald_atelier).

A post shared by Vanessa 👩🏻 (@little_inkdrops).

A post shared by StayKpopPrints (@staykpopprints).

For years, Etsy has been one of the best places to sell art and design online, particularly handmade craft items, from jewelry and gifts made with Cricut machines to illustration and poster design. But like many platforms, it's faced the problem of quality products being drowned out by AI slop and copied art posted by bots.

The new terms come into effect on 16 December, and they've sparked an exodus from the platform. Many creatives have taken to social media to announce the closure of their Etsy stores, using flyers and goodbye letters created in their signature art styles.

According to recent reports, some speak of wrestling over a decision that they fear could harm their business in the short term. Others who have yet to take the leap say they feel trapped because they depend on Etsy as their main source of income and the patch has come at the most crucial time of the year for sales.

Like with Cara for social media, alternative specifically anti-AI marketplaces like Marmalade Handmade, but they remain small compared to Etsy. Some sellers say they can't leave the platform yet but are taking the step of writing to customers to ask them to shop with them directly instead of using the platform.

In an patch on the Etsy Community site this week, VP of Customer Operations James Ossman stressed that sellers retain ownership of their creative work on Etsy that the company was focusing on using AI to support sellers and improve the Etsy experience.

In a recent development, he writes: "We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers.".

He provided some examples of how the platform is training AI, including to identify potentially fraudulent accounts and related listings, to understand inventory, to help buyers find items and tailored recommendations and to build tools to help sellers run their businesses more efficiently.

He mentioned Etsy uses security tools to detect and limit unauthorised scraping, while its terms prohibit unauthorised use of marketplace content for AI training. However, he doesn't specify whether authorised partners can use seller content to train models for applications unrelated to Etsy, and the platform has not provider a general opt-out mechanism for sellers who don't want their content used for AI training.

It may be that sellers have nothing to fear, in which case Etsy should really have tried to find a better way to communicate the update. It's aware of the sensitivity around AI, and it's natural for sellers to be frightened by the language in the upcoming terms at a time when AI is being used to clone artists' work in a multitude of fields, from illustration to video game development.

It has been revealed that are you concerned about Etsy's AI policy? Let us know in the comments.

Tech Report: Christie’s Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At its packed Rockefeller Center saleroom on Tuesday night, Christie’s staged a sometimes lively, sometimes listless two-hour-and-40-minute sale of 20th-century art, led by an $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt.
